title: Discharge capacitors safely
summary: Build a resistor discharge tool with insulated leads, use it to drain dangerous capacitors in microwaves, power supplies, inverters and air conditioners, then prove they are empty with a meter. Do this every time, even if the device has been unplugged for months.

materials.item: Wire-wound or ceramic power resistor, 2–5 kΩ, 10 W or more, for capacitors up to about 450 V
For kilovolt capacitors such as microwave ones: ten 10 kΩ resistors of 2 W or more, joined end to end (about 100 kΩ)
Rigid plastic pipe or dry wooden dowel about 30 cm long, for the handle
Short jumper wire with insulated clips at both ends

steps.text: Build the tool once and keep it. Solder the resistor, or the chain of resistors end to end, inside the plastic pipe. One end connects to a short metal probe tip sticking out of the end of the pipe. The other end connects to 1 m of insulated wire with an insulated crocodile clip. Seal both ends with tape or heat-shrink.
steps.warn: No bare metal except the probe tip and the clip jaws. Never use a metal tube as the handle.

steps.text: Unplug the device, or disconnect its battery. Wait at least 5 minutes. Take off the cover without touching anything inside.
steps.warn: Unplugged does not mean safe. Capacitors can hold a lethal charge for days.

steps.text: Find every capacitor that matters. Look for big cylinders and metal cans and read their labels (µF and V). In a microwave it is the metal can beside the big transformer. Power supplies often have two or more.
steps.warn: Treat any capacitor rated over 50 V as charged until you have measured it.

steps.text: Take off rings and your watch. Stand on a dry floor. Put one hand in your pocket and keep it there for the next steps.
Clip the tool's lead to one capacitor terminal, holding only the insulated body of the clip.
steps.warn: Touch one terminal only. Never let your fingers bridge both terminals.

steps.text: Holding the plastic handle well back from the tip, touch the probe to the other terminal and hold it there for at least 10 seconds. A small spark or click is normal.
steps.warn: If you get a big bang or the tool smokes, the resistor is too small for the job. Stop and build a bigger one.

steps.text: Move the clip to bare metal on the chassis and touch the probe to each capacitor terminal in turn for 5 seconds. Some circuits store charge between a terminal and the case.
Set the meter to DC volts and measure across the terminals. It should read under 1 V. Then measure each terminal to the chassis.
steps.warn: If it reads more than a few volts, discharge again. Don't touch anything until it reads near zero.

steps.text: Clip the jumper wire across the capacitor terminals and leave it there while you work.
steps.warn: Large capacitors can creep back up to a dangerous voltage after being drained.

steps.text: If you leave the job and come back, discharge and measure again. When you take a capacitor out, twist a bare wire across its terminals before storing it.

notes:
## Why a resistor and not a screwdriver

A screwdriver across the terminals dumps all the stored energy in an instant. That makes a loud arc, sprays molten metal, pits the tip, can damage the capacitor inside, and puts your hand a few centimetres from the terminals. It also gives you no proof the job worked. A resistor drains the charge in a second or two at a safe current, lets you stand back, and the meter then proves it.

## Sizing the resistor

| Capacitor | Typical label | Resistor | Hold for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Power supply, UPS, inverter and TV electrolytics | up to 450 V | 2–5 kΩ, 10 W or more | 10 s |
| Motor run and start capacitors (AC units, pumps, fans) | 250–450 VAC | 2–5 kΩ, 10 W or more | 10 s |
| Camera flash | about 300 V | 2–5 kΩ, 10 W or more | 5 s |
| Microwave oven capacitor | about 1 µF, 2,000 VAC or more | chain of ten 10 kΩ, 2 W each | 10 s |
| Motor drives (VFDs), solar and EV inverters, big welders: the DC bus | 400–900 V DC, often thousands of µF | chain of four 1 kΩ, 25 W or more each (metal-clad) | 60 s |

**Time:** a capacitor is close to empty after about five time constants. One time constant is R × C (ohms × farads = seconds). Example: 470 µF through 2 kΩ is about 0.9 s, so about 5 s to near zero. A microwave capacitor through 100 kΩ is about 0.1 s. Holding for 10 s gives a big margin.

**Voltage rating:** a small resistor can only stand a few hundred volts across it. At 2 kV it flashes over and behaves like a short. That is why the microwave tool uses a chain: ten resistors in series each see about a tenth of the voltage.

**Current:** peak current is volts divided by ohms. 400 V through 2 kΩ is 0.2 A, which the tool handles easily. The resistor warms up after big capacitors; let it cool between jobs.

## Meter limits

Most handheld meters are rated 600 V or 1,000 V; anything near a 600 V reading needs the 1,000 V kind. Never put one on a capacitor that might hold more than that. Always discharge first, then measure.

## Motor drives and big inverters

A motor drive (VFD), a grid-tie or EV inverter or a big welder rectifies mains into a DC bus of 400–900 V across a bank of large capacitors: hundreds of joules, enough to kill and to blow a small tool apart.

- The drive’s label or cover says how long to wait after switching off, often 5–15 minutes, while its own bleeders drain the bus. Wait at least that long, then wait again if the charge light on the board is still lit.
- Find the DC bus terminals (often marked + and −, P and N, or DC+ and DC−) and measure across them with a meter rated 1,000 V (CAT III or better) before touching anything.
- Only if it still reads over 50 V, drain it with the four-resistor chain above: each resistor sees about a quarter of the voltage, and the chain gets hot, so hold it for 60 seconds, let it cool, and measure again.
- If the bus reads over 1,000 V, or you can’t find it, close the cover and leave it.

## Supercapacitors

Supercapacitors are low voltage (often 2.7 V a cell) but can deliver huge currents. They won't shock you, but shorting one can melt a wire or a ring. Drain them through a low-value resistor (1–10 Ω, a few watts) and measure.

## Common mistakes

- Trusting the bleed resistor. Many capacitors have one, and they fail.
- Draining one capacitor and forgetting the second one on the same board.
- Measuring on AC volts. Use DC volts on a stored charge.
- Holding the lead near the clip instead of by the handle.
- Skipping the meter check because "it sparked, so it's empty".
